newsitem.title: USA: Fed raises interest rates, first time in two years.
newsitem.headline: Fed raises interest rates, first time in two years.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent

The U.S. Federal Reserve on Tuesday raised interest rates for the first time in more than two years in a politically controversial move to stay a step ahead of inflation and keep the economic expansion on track.
The quarter-percentage-point increase by the central bank means higher borrowing costs for a variety of consumers and companies, from credit card users to the stores they shop at.

Several banks, including Banc One of Columbus, Ohio, and Citibank of New York, quickly matched the Fed's move, boosting their prime lending rate for business customers to 8.50 percent from 8.25 percent. Others are expected to follow suit.
The Fed described its rate rise as a "prudent step" designed to help prolong the economic expansion by keeping inflation low through the end of next year.
"This action was taken in light of persisting strength in demand, which is progressively increasing the risk of inflationary imbalances developing in the economy," it added.

The Fed increased its target for the federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans to 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent. It left the discount rate that it charges the banks for money unchanged at 5.0 percent.
The rate rise, the first by the Fed since February 1995, drew fire from companies and Congressmen who argued it would slow the economy at a time when inflation was already low.
"In one fell swoop, the Fed has taken money out of the pockets of every family, small business and farm in America," Democratic Senator Tom Harkin of Iowa said.

The Clinton administration though shied away from criticising the independent central bank and voiced confidence that the six-year-old economic expansion will continue with low inflation and low unemplyment.
"We believe that the economy will continue on this path, led by strong private sector investment," Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and White House economist Janet Yellen said.
Financial markets gyrated in response to the Fed move as investors tried to weigh the likelihood of further rate rises.

The Dow Jones industrial average of blue chip shares closed 29.08 points lower at 6,876.17. The 30-year Treasury bond lost about a half percentage point, or some $5 per $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.97 percent from 6.92 percent.

Analysts were divided over the Fed's next move. Many believe central bank policy-makers will raise rates at least one more time, possibly as soon as their next meeting on May 20, to slow down the economy and head off inflation.

"Usually they raise rates a number of times ... Normally when they start raising rates they end up raising them by at least one percent," said William Ford, a former President of the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta.

But other Fed watchers were not so sure that Tuesday's action presaged a series of rate increases by the central bank and argued that the economy was likely to cool off on its own without much, if any, further help from the Fed.
"I view this as a mid-course correction,' said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist of Minneapolis-based Norwest Corp. "I don't expect this to lead to a series of tightenings."

After expanding at a brisk 3.9 percent annualized pace in the fourth quarter of last year, the economy looks to have slowed slightly in the first three months of this year to a growth rate closer to three percent, analysts said.
Much of the slowdown has occured in the so-called external sector, as U.S. exports have sagged and imports have soared, in part because the strong dollar has made foreign goods cheaper.

Domestic U.S. demand has stayed strong, although special factors may have played a role there. This winter has been much warmer than last, spurring construction. And consumer spending has been boosted by larger-than-normal tax refunds.
Greenspan told lawmakers last week that the economy retains a "great deal of vigor" and termed the prospects for a continuation of the six-year-old expansion "quite favourable."
But he also made clear that depended critically on the Fed staying ahead of inflation and keeping it from rising.
Greenspan pointed to the tight jobs market in particular as a potential source of concern, voicing worries that it could lead to excessive wage demands and spiralling inflation.
He has also singled out the buoyant stock market for attention. The Fed is worried that equity prices may have risen too far and may be a harbinger of higher inflation.
Fed critics though argued that the central bank should have waited before pulling the trigger on a rate rise.
"With no inflation in the current data, and few, if any signs of future inflation, we believe the Fed had room to wait," U.S. Chamber of Commerce Chamber's Martin Regalia said.
"Clearly the pressure to raise rates came from the brokerage houses on Wall Street, not the small businesses on Main Street," the business group's chief economist added.
Tuesday's rate increase marked a reversal of Fed policy. Its last rate change came on Jan. 31, 1996, when it trimmed rates by a quarter percentage point.
